comments.text: Correction! A number of folks in the comments pointed out that research exists proving that honing does, in fact, remove metal from the blade. I went back and did some reading of my own and issued a correction via my Patreon. Read it for free here: https://frienji.kenjilopezalt.com/posts/how-honing-fixes-168800580?pr=true

Kenji, I recently went to Japan as well and one of the highlights of my trips was a visit to the Natural Whetstone Museam in Kameoka, Kyoto. The staff were amazing! I paid for a lesson on how to sharpen single bevel knives and it was extremely gratifying. Highly recommend for your next trip if you've never been. I now own 3 natural stones that i consider dear treasures from that trip.

If you can buy just one stone in the beginning i.e. you want something cheap and flexible, I'd go for something like Shapton Kuromaku 1000. It's perhaps a bit more effective/rougher than your average 1000 grit, and if your blade doesn't need reshaping and serious chip fixing, it'll do the job easily. And it's wonderful to use because it's splash 'n' go stone, you don't have to soak it in a water bath for a period of time before using it. And the cost is very affordable, one of the more affordable stones. Using just one stone like that also helps a lot in when you're a beginner and nobody is observing your work, telling you what's going on, and you think you sharpened enough and move to another stone and perhaps even to a third stone, and then your knife still doesn't cut anything and you wonder what's happening. And you just have no clue about if you should move to another stone or not and where the problem was. With just one stone you can fully focus on just the skill of hand and realize that it's "all" in your own control of movement instead of handling the equipment.

What I'd really avoid is those seemingly great bang for the buck combo stones you can sometimes find in regular stores. For example 400/800 or 1000/4000 or whatever. They are usually very poor quality and extremely muddy, my experience is that with one of those it feels like you're doing it in a bouncy castle full of mud - your knife just removes the stone instead of the other way around and with all the mud you can't get much feeling of your work. And they wear out fast as well. With a hard single grit stone the cost is a little bit higher, but you don't need many to get good results and they will last a long time. For a hobbyist they might almost be life time stones. So it pays off to consider the cost over time.

For a beginner, per my personal experience, the angle is really not that big of a deal to stress about. If you feel like it's roughly making a narrowing tip that resembles a knife edge in your mind, it's probably good enough. The biggest thing is consistency of hand movement. It took me a couple of times to start getting anything that resembled sharpened, just because my hands wouldn't keep a consistent angle and as consequence the edge wasn't consistently getting narrower until it's just a thin ridge, it would be rounded geometry. And I was getting quite frustrated because I couldn't understand what I was doing wrong when my knife wasn't getting sharp, let alone shaving sharp. It's just a skill that you need to hone by doing, it isn't enough that you know what and how you should be doing, you just have to repeat it until your hands do it.

Once you can make pretty consistent sharpening movement and you have the perception and feel to when you didn't quite follow it successfully, and you start observing the change of the blade - meaning the formation of the burr (and perhaps feeling when the edge is sharp enough to bite your finger or nail) - that's when I've noticed I don't even pay much attention to the angle. The range of an effective angle is so wide as long as you're able to form the good consistent edge that it really isn't a big factor for how sharp you get your knives. It might become easy to chip if it's ridiculously low angle, or hard to get through items even though it's sharp if the angle is very big, but generally you get a roughly good angle and the bigger question is if you can even form the sharp edge.

Another thing that was a difficult thing for me was not having pressure on the blade. It was doing the light passes that get lighter and lighter to clean the burr so that you "finish" the edge and it doesn't lose its cutting ability after a while because the ripping burr was chipped because you minimized it. And that usually is the difference at least for me for a knife that seems like it has a good edge but sucks at cutting, and a knife that actually makes you careful because it bites easy.

And you can help a lot on average, not that expensive, kitchen knife by just making the secondary bevel. That means the angle behind your edge angle. A lot of knives tend to have a bit of a thick spine to give them sturdiness, but often times that thickness continues all the way until the edge bevel. What you want to do is you want to create a sort of intermediary sector, another angle between the spine thickness and the edge bevel. That thinned out section behind the edge bevel allows the knife to split through items after the knife cuts in and helps the cutting efficiency a ton. I wouldn't have believed its effect until I tried to do it on my cheap kitchen knife that had a sharp edge but still felt a bit tough to use. When you have that secondary bevel, the knife just happily slides through the items. And it allows you to preserve a bit of thickness behind the edge for support so it's not as likely to chip because you thinned out the edge bevel so much.

Personally I prefer the technique on the passes that goes through the whole blade at once, just because I'm not that confident in my perception and evenness of doing it section by section and being consistent. A great way to test the sharpness of the knife is having something like a tomato on a surface that has some friction, and cutting a fine slice horizontally without holding the tomato. If the tomato doesn't get pushed away but instead the edge bites and you can slide for a slice, that's how you know it cuts well. Or if you can similarly shave your arm hair without pressure. It doesn't need to be polished with high grit for that, just having been sharpened to a good geometry and the burr removed.

Before lapping the stone, if you want to be sure you're not missing a spot or don't know how even your stone actually is (sometimes from the factory they can be quite surprisingly shaped on the surface) a really handy trick is to draw a hash mesh on the stone with a pencil (let's say about inch gaps to give some perspective). Then as you lap the stone, you can see the pencil markings disappear and discover at the same time where you haven't managed to touch the surface yet, and how off shaped your stone was. Once all the pencil markings are gone, you know you have cleared the surface and all its mountains and valleys.

And it might be handy to do the same as Kenji's stones seemed to already have: lap the edges of the stone with 45 degree chamfer. It helps you avoid catching the sharper edge with the blade and making an annoying dent you have to fix, and I suppose it also makes the stone less prone to chipping if you drop it (after all the edges are focused tension spots).

To me it's not even how much material those home gadgets take away. It's having seen the microscopic images of the work they do. It's like putting your knife through a wood chipper. You can't really call it sharpening, it just makes your knife like a ripper instead of cutter. And as the random burrs chip off, you're left with a dull knife potentially the next day. The same effect I had when I bought a diamond honing rod when I didn't understand honing rods and their purpose. If your honing rod has that much material removal power, you're ripping the edge and ruining it. If it's like a ceramic one, you're barely doing anything (it's not a sharpener) but you're potentially cleaning the edge. So after a bit of experimenting and learning, I ended up with just whetstones. The rest were just wasted money. But having a strop (with a sturdy support like the leather on a wood plank) and perhaps even stropping substance (be it regular stick or diamond paste) can be a really nice way to clean the burr at the end of sharpening. And the whetstones and a strop can make even your cheap super market knife cut so well that you don't care to invest in an expensive nice with stronger metals.

And one of the best things about sharp knife is that you don't need a "bread knife", you can cut through soft bread without trouble and you don't crush onions or other veggies so they don't start producing chemicals or get discoloured or whatever each individual veggie does when the cells are crushed.
Those knifes skills at the end!! 😍

More importantly, if you want to retain your edge, use a strop AFTER sharpening, it removes the bur and gives you an actually good edge, a lot of people sharpen and leave the bur on, thinking the knife is sharp, but the bur is actually doing the majority of the cutting and wears out in a very short period of time since it's basically just tiny little metal flakes doing the cutting rather than actually using the edge of the knife

One also gets used to the sound of a knife on the stone. A change in the knife angle sounds different. A change in pressure and grinding vs skating knife sound different too. Over time the auditory memory builds like the muscle memory for control on wrist/finger/pressure.

Instead of the towel, I use a cheap silicon baking mat that I have cut down for an odd sized baking sheet. Not silpat style. Just silicon with no weave. Works great and I can wash and use for baking later. Never do, but I can!

Another really good, and cheap, option is a thick piece of plate glass and wet/dry silicon carbide sandpaper that you attach to the glass using spray on temporary adhesive. This is an approach a lot of woodworkers use to keep their chisels (and similar tools) sharp. Modern plate glass is incredibly flat and the sandpaper can simply be replaced with a new sheet when it no longer does the job. No need to do whetstone maintenance to keep it flat.

If I only had one stone and it couldn't be a diamond plate, I'd probably go with the Naniwa Chosera 800. Been using one for about 10 years now, Cuts pretty quickly and in the right hands, creates razor-sharp edges. Great all around splash-and-go stone. For me, the ultimate budget "stones" are diamond plates, like the ones from Sharpal. They profile and sharpen amazingly quick, but the trade-off is feel, Sharpal does a pretty good job adhering the diamonds to the plate, so they last a long time. If you're on a budget and insist on actual whetstones, King makes a combination stone with 1000/6000 grit that works quite well, but I'd pair it with an inexpensive 400 grit diamond stone for rapid profiling. Oh, and learn to strop. If you can afford a nice leather one, great, but in a pinch, corrugated cardboard boxes do a decent job.

I'm gonna be honest I don't really think whetstone sharpening is the play for 99% of home cooks or even really professional cooks. It's something really for "knife sharpening enthusiasts" or people who sharpen knives for a living but for the average person, the mess and hassle of soaking the stones, laying them out, and making a mess and then also having to occasionally maintain the stones themselves and re-flatten them, it's all really not worth it? If you must sharpen free  hand, the diamond sharpening stones are just so much less hassle for what is essentially an equivalent tool that requires much less maintenance, but even then, I think most people are better off getting some kind of sharpening system with a jig that removes the free hand portion of of the equation. Why? Because angle consistency is the most important part and most people will not spend the dozens of hours required doing nothing but sharpening to be able to consistently hold an angle free hand. It's why most people try it once or twice, get frustrated when they don't get the results they are looking for and give up. Or they try it, and end up with a "sharp knife" that's only sharp for a few uses because it has a sharp bur and then falsely equate that to them having a new found talent for knife sharpening, but then they wonder why they have to do it weekly.  Really you are better off either using a stone-based fixed angle sharpening system or a belt based one with a jig for holding a fixed angle. If it's easier and faster and yields what is most likely a superior result for 99% of people, you will be more likely to pull it out to maintain your knives than a whetstone system that fills you with dread every time you think about dealing with the hassle and mess.

Nice tutorial! I'm a nerd and so I tend to get into the weeds with these things, so I'm going to nitpick a couple details. I promise it comes from a good place!

Whenever the topic of honing and honing rods comes up I really like to direct people to a research site called "Science of Sharp." The site is written by a scientific researcher who used electron microscopic photography to show what sharpness looks like, and how various methods and tools of sharpening affect the apex of a blade on the microscopic level. Their article, "What does steeling do?" is of particular interest here. 

The thing we hear constantly about honing rods is that they don't sharpen, they don't remove material, they only "re-align the edge" of a knife. However, if you've ever used a ribbed steel honing rod and swiped it with a damp towel, you can see this is not quite accurate. The towel will show the same dark sediment that you will see left behind on a whetstone. We call that "swarf," microscopic metal shavings, evidence of removal of material. This evidence is even more pronounced when using a ceramic rod, the dark streaks of swarf left on a white ceramic surface are unmistakable. 

This is also evident in the microscope photography provided by SoS's article, and they make two things clear. One, that moderate dullness is not merely caused by a misaligned edge, but also by microscopic chipping and flattened surfaces at the edge's apex. And two, that this damage cannot be fixed with "realignment." A new keen edge must be formed by removal of material. Honing rods do this by creating a new micro-bevel at the apex, restoring that keen edge. 

While it is true that you cannot use a honing rod to resharpen a knife with a fully rounded apex, this does not mean that honing rods do not remove material, they are simply too fine a tool for that task. Nonetheless, it is evident that honing rods remove some material, and they remove steel by way of "adhesive wear." This is in contrast to how other sharpening tools remove steel, which is typically "abrasive wear", e.g. "grinding" away the material. 

This doesn't change how we performing honing in contrast to sharpening, most people can (and probably will) go on believing that honing rods only realign edges and still benefit from the keen edges they restore. But I think it's good to know what is actually happening based on the evidence instead of long held word of mouth. If you agree, check out the images and see for yourself!
